templates.stem: Find the set of ordered pairs (x, y) which satisfy the relation $y = 2x - 1$ when $x = 0$, $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. Tap the pairs that satisfy the relation.
solution: Take each value of x in turn: 0, 1 and 2.
For x = 0: y = 2(0) - 1 = -1, so the pair is (0, -1).
For x = 1: y = 2(1) - 1 = 1, so the pair is (1, 1).
For x = 2: y = 2(2) - 1 = 3, so the pair is (2, 3).
The set is {(0, -1), (1, 1), (2, 3)}, with x first and y second in each pair.

hints.text: There is one pair for each value of x you were given. Check that every one of them has a pair.
Substitute each x into $y = 2x - 1$ and compute y. Only a pair whose y matches that result belongs in the set.

templates.notes: Relation mode: every pair of X×Y is on the board, the stem states only the rule.

templates.stem: Represent the ordered pairs (0, -1), (1, 1) and (2, 3) graphically in the coordinate plane. Tap each point.
solution: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis vertical, meeting at O.
Plot (0, -1): at 0 on the x-axis, then 1 unit down.
Plot (1, 1): 1 unit right, 1 unit up.
Plot (2, 3): 2 units right, 3 units up.
Each ordered pair is one and only one point.

hints.text: Each ordered pair in the list gives one point. Check that every pair has been plotted.
Only the pairs listed are plotted. Check each point against the pairs, moving along x first and then along y.
Check the direction for each move: right or left along x, then up or down along y, as the signs say.

templates.stem: On a perpendicular graphical net representing Q on both axes, plot the point $A(3,\frac{5}{2})$. Tap the point.
solution: Move 3 units right along the x-axis.
Move 2.5 units up, halfway between 2 and 3.
Mark the point.

hints.text: The first number is the position along the horizontal axis and the second is the height.
Check the sign of each number to see which way to move.
Write the fraction as a decimal first, then count along each axis in steps of one half.

templates.stem: If $X=[-2,3]$, mark the location which represents $X\times X$. Drag two opposite corners onto the grid and set each edge solid (included) or dashed (excluded).
solution: X × X is the set of pairs (x, y) with x in [-2, 3] and y in [-2, 3].
So x runs from -2 to 3 along the horizontal axis.
And y runs from -2 to 3 along the vertical axis.
The interval is closed, so every edge is included (solid).
The region is a square with corners (-2, -2) and (3, 3).

hints.text: The interval [-2, 3] has square brackets. Decide whether each edge should be solid or dashed.
Both coordinates of a pair in X × X come from the same interval. Mark where x and y can each lie.

templates.notes: Book parts A-D are yes/no membership checks on this location; this template covers the construction in the stem, attached to part A.

gaps.description: think-3: represent N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R on a graphical net
gaps.why: The products are infinite sets with an open-ended description. No widget grades an infinite lattice, a dense set, or a whole plane as a drawing, and the book gives no specific points.

templates.stem: If $X=\{1,2,3\}$, $Y=\{12,21,47,52\}$ and R is the relation from X to Y where a R b means: a is a digit of b, for each $a\in X$, $b\in Y$. Represent R by an arrow diagram: tap an element of X, then the element of Y it is related to.
solution: Take each a in X in turn and look at the digits of every b in Y.
1 is a digit of 12 and of 21, so draw arrows 1 → 12 and 1 → 21.
2 is a digit of 12, 21 and 52, so draw arrows 2 → 12, 2 → 21 and 2 → 52.
3 is a digit of none of 12, 21, 47, 52, so no arrow leaves 3.
R = {(1, 12), (1, 21), (2, 12), (2, 21), (2, 52)}, and the arrow diagram shows exactly these five arrows.

hints.text: Go through each element of X one at a time and check it against the digits of every element of Y, so no related element is skipped.
An arrow is drawn only when a is really a digit of b. Re-read the digits of each b you have joined.
Arrows go from the element of X (the first in the pair) to the element of Y (the second).

templates.notes: The cartesian-diagram part of this exercise is a gap (see gaps). Second part is a judgement of given pairs, not a construction.

gaps.why: Student must write a set of ordered pairs. product_builder relation mode is limited to 4 numbers per set and numbers only (here 5 students × 4 book types, words), and the statements are on a previous page. No kind fits.

gaps.description: think-and-discuss-2: represent a set of ordered pairs as an arrow diagram.
gaps.why: The stem does not say which ordered pairs (they come from the previous activity), so the widget could not stand alone and its key cannot be read from the stem.

gaps.description: drill-1 First (cartesian diagram part): plot R = {(1,12),(1,21),(2,12),(2,21),(2,52)}.
gaps.why: pair_plotter needs lattice points on a grid of at most 16 steps per axis; y values 12, 21 and 52 cannot all sit on a step of one board that reaches 52 (a step of 1 would need 52 steps), so no grid holds them.

gaps.description: pp3u1-3:think-and-discuss-1: Write each relation and represent it by a cartesian diagram.
gaps.why: The relations are in the book's figures. Their sets and pairs are not in the exercise text, so a spec would have to use numbers I made up. pair_plotter could plot a cartesian diagram, but only once the pairs are known. The worked example's f on {3,4,5,6} is a different problem, so I did not substitute it.

records.notes: I wrote no templates for this lesson. drill-1, drill-2 and think-and-discuss-2 ask the student to pick which diagrams are functions. That is reading figures, not building anything. think-1 is an open explanation. Objective 3 (domain, codomain and range) has no exercises. The only construction exercise is think-and-discuss-1, and I recorded it as a gap because its relations are not given.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=2\frac{1}{2}$. Draw the graph freehand across the whole board.
solution: The rule is $f(x)=2.5$: every $x$ has the same image, so this is a constant function.
Mark these points on the square net: they all lie at the same height.
Draw the straight line through them, parallel to the x-axis and meeting the y-axis at $(0, 2.5)$.

hints.text: Look at the table of values: what is the image of every x? Check the height at which your line meets the y-axis.
The domain is all of R, so the line should run across the whole visible board, not stop part-way.
A function gives one image for each x. Draw a single line moving from left to right without doubling back.
Start from the rule: does the image change when x changes? Use that to decide the direction of the line.

templates.notes: Line_drawer needs whole b, so the half-valued constant uses the freehand linear curve_sketcher on the default board (2.5 is within −5..5).

records.notes: Other exercises (identify polynomials, find degree, evaluate values, prove f(3)=g(3)=0, think-and-discuss) are readings or calculations, not constructions, so no gaps.
